title_en: Auckland hit by swarms of bees after milder than usual New Zealand winter
excerpt_en: Beekeepers say they are fielding a record number of calls from people needing assistance in removing swarms
body_en: Engulfing parked cars and blanketing inner-city street signs – New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland, is in the midst of an unusually large bee swarming season, that experts say has been exacerbated by a milder than usual winter.

The Auckland Beekeepers Association says it is fielding five to 10 calls a day, requesting assistance to remove swarms of bees – with individual members of the association being contacted for help as well.
“In past years, it was under five a day,” said Bryan Lang, the association’s swarm control coordinator, adding the team has now dealt with at least 100 call-outs.
In October, a swarm plastered the back of a parked car in Birkenhead for two hours according to witnesses. A woman inside was napping at the time, Lang understands.
“I’m surprised she didn’t hear them because they’re pretty loud,” he said.
Related: The night-sky image so incredible the NZ man behind it has been accused of using AI
A month earlier, a swarm took over a sign at a busy intersection on Auckland’s major commercial thoroughfare, Queen Street, forcing pedestrians to reroute.

During spring and early summer, bees can “swarm” – a natural occurrence which sees part of a colony that has outgrown its hive abandon it in search of a new home or extra food. The mass of insects will temporarily find a place to land away from their hive, while scout bees search for an appropriate dwelling.

“As a beekeeper, you don’t want them to swarm because you’re losing two-thirds of your bees, and right at the time when they should be bringing honey in for you,” said Lang. “And it’s not great for your neighbours either.”

Public awareness is growing over why bees swarm, and what to do should one happen to take over part of your garden or street, and according to Lang, many are taking to social media bee swarming pages and local beekeeping clubs to appeal for help.
The association’s president, Ken Brown, says when bees swarm in the countryside, no one really notices, but “townies” are not so familiar.

“If you don’t know about bees – how they’re only defensive – then you might be intimidated with thousands of venomous insects flying around,” he said, adding that a colony of bees is at its most placid when swarming.

Brown believes a much milder winter and start to spring has led to bees swarming weeks earlier than usual, and larger numbers of bees splitting off from their hives. New Zealand experienced its third warmest winter on record in 2026, according to Earth Sciences NZ. Other parts of the world are seeing similar behavioural shifts in bees, including in North America, as global warming leads to hotter winters and spring.

“Beekeeping is much more unpredictable nowadays because you do have the extremes of weather and the different patterns. Every year is slightly different, but it’s actually even more different in recent times,” said Brown.

Milder temperatures over winter might mean a colony develops a larger brood of eggs, larvae and pupae. If they don’t succumb to varroa mite, a tiny and deadly parasite that attaches to honeybees and their brood, then the survivors will be “much stronger and ready to swarm sooner”, said Brown.
Prof Phil Lester, an etymologist and ecologist at Victoria University, said beekeepers have been active catching swarms in other parts of the country, including Wellington.

Unmanaged bee swarms that cannot be captured pose a risk to other honeybees or native bees if they are carrying varroa mite. Further, it can be a pain for beekeepers to lose their bees right when they are readying to produce honey.
Still, it could be a positive signal for this year’s bee populations, Lester said.
“It means they have been able to build up numbers and populations, earlier than perhaps they normally would do … its probably a good indication that it is a good bee year.”

title_en: Can Gadi Eisenkot turn the ‘disaster bloc’ into Israel’s next government?
excerpt_en: With deep political divisions at home and multiple crises abroad, forming a government – and keeping it together – won’t be easy.
body_en: Amir Levy/Getty On Sunday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced he would grant Gadi Eisenkot – main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – the opportunity to form a new government in Israel.
It followed almost a fortnight of political gridlock, after what has been called the “most consequential election in Israel’s history” failed to produce a clear winner.
Eisenkot now has 28 days (with a possible 14-day extension) to attempt to convene a stable coalition government. He’ll have to bring together a deeply divided opposition.
Even if he succeeds, his government will face major challenges – including keeping his coalition together, a changing relationship with the United States, and escalating violence in the West Bank.
Read more: Israel election by the numbers: who might form the next government?

An extraordinary election In Israeli elections, it is standard practice for the president to formally nominate who should bring a coalition government together. This does not have to be the leader of the party that has secured the most votes – in this case, Netanyahu.
Israel’s voting system is intrinsically geared toward producing coalition governments. The country has never had a one-party government.
Netanyahu’s Likud party won the highest number of seats in Israel’s election on October 27. But his coalition lacked the 61 seats required for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
The parties in opposition to Netanyahu – led by Eisenkot – also lacked the numbers to form a governing coalition.
Meanwhile, the two Arab-majority parties representing the interests of two million citizens of Israel (the Joint List and Ra’am) received 19 seats between them – more than ever before.
While the procedure that has given Eisenkot a chance to become Israel’s new prime minister is standard practice, the conditions in which this election has taken place are historically fraught.
This is the first time Israelis have gone to the polls since Hamas’ shocking attack of October 7 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza that followed.
Many challenging questions are raised by the fact that, at this momentous time in the history of the Jewish nation-state, the electoral process has ended inconclusively.
A new Israeli government, dependent on Arab parties? The election outcome was made much more complicated by the tension between numbers and politics.

To form a potential governing coalition, Eisenkot’s Yashar party could be joined by Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, Yair Golan’s Democrats and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu. But to achieve a majority in parliament, they would need at least one the two Arab parties to join a historically broad unity government.
Doing so, however, would require Eisenkot – and Bennett and Liberman – to go against campaign promises that they would not enter into coalition with the Arab parties.

This leaves Eisenkot in a difficult position. The support of these two Arab parties could help break the political deadlock. But it could also make what is already an improbable coalition of Israeli parties fall apart before it even starts governing.
The need for political cooperation and unity in Israel today is perhaps greater than ever before. Eisenkot has emphasised that “all of us will need to compromise”.

But compromising in principle needs to be possible in practice. A multi-party government that relies formally or informally on two different Arab parties may not be a feasible basis for political renewal in Israel.
Observing the political dilemma facing their opponents, members of Netanyahu’s Likud party have referred to them as “the disaster bloc”.
Coalition conundrums There is no question that the enlarged parliamentary presence of the two Arab parties is significant. It poses fundamental questions about the nature of Israel’s democracy.

Israel’s 2018 Nation-State Law states that “the right of national self-determination in the state of Israel is unique to the Jewish people”. This makes it difficult for Arab parties to represent the national self-determination interests of Palestinians while also supporting an Israeli government.

title_en: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
excerpt_en: Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’
body_en: OpenAI won’t face criminal penalties over the Medicare hack but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.
Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach but not the findings or the report itself.

A key recommendation is for the attorney general’s department, the Australian federal police and home affairs to consider reforming the law to introduce “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.
Related: An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so far
The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting, including but not limited to misaligned behaviour or agentic cyber incidents”.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told reporters “we need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do”.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately,” Burke said in Canberra alongside the PM.
On the “concept of looking at how we can update our criminal law”, Burke said: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.”
“We need to make sure that the criminal law is up to date for how this new technology is able to act.”
Albanese on Tuesday characterised OpenAI’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy.
“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” the prime minister told reporters in Canberra.
“All of that was confirmed essentially … but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”
The review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.
Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place.
AI researcher Toby Walsh said the people in charge of these companies needed to be criminally liable to ensure they did the right thing.
“We’ve tried fining them, and we’re not the only ones. These companies are incredibly wealthy, and it’s almost impossible to fine them enough,” he said.
The AI agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June.
The company didn’t notify the Australian government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August.
Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.
Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator.
Labor would consider six key obligations on AI companies, including:
maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment;

title_en: Ukraine war briefing: battlefield gains bolstering Kyiv’s hand in US-led peace talks, Zelenskyy says
excerpt_en: Ukrainian president says battlefield successes and mounting Russian losses add to negotiating leverage ahead of Abu Dhabi talks on Tuesday. What we know on day 1,721
body_en: Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy has said ⁠that battlefield ‌successes ‌were strengthening Kyiv’s position ‌in negotiations, on ⁠the ⁠eve of new US-led trilateral talks ⁠on resolving the war. “Every task that is fully accomplished, every ⁠defensive operation that increases Ukraine’s strength and delivers results, strengthens Ukraine ‌and, above all, strengthens us in negotiations,” the president said in his nightly video address on Monday. Zelenskyy said top Ukrainian military commander Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented ‌a report that underscored heavy recent losses by Russian forces. He added that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on ‌Russian targets, including oil industry sites, were also working.

Russia’s battlefield losses have reached levels unprecedented in its modern history, according to data shared with the Guardian’s Pjotr Sauer. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine over nearly five years of fighting, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat. The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, shows 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.

US negotiators in Tuesday’s Abu Dhabi talks believe that Zelenskyy and Russian president Vladimir Putin may be willing to strike a compromise on ‌the vital question of territory, with each ceding a little, an American official told Reuters. Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to accession to the EU. In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on Sunday, Donald Trump said Ukraine would have “a little bit different shape” under the settlement, but he didn’t elaborate. A senior Ukrainian official strongly denied that the government would consider any such concessions.

Trump on Monday said that Washington was seeing a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting.” However, US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave a more sober assessment of peace efforts. Rubio said the process still has “ways to go”, and that getting Europeans to the table with the Russians has still not happened. “It’s been difficult to get anything productive out of that,” Rubio told reporters a day before the talks.

European powers, ⁠including France, Germany and the European Commission, ⁠will send officials to the talks, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations. Instead, Ukrainian delegates will meet separately to brief their European allies on progress. “We are doing everything to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process,” Rustem Umerov, the head of the Ukrainian delegation, said on Monday.

EU foreign ministers pressed Rubio at a G7 meeting in Paris to ensure Europe is represented at the negotiations. German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said after talks with Rubio: “Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe.” Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday that Trump’s team had placed “collective security”, covering not just Russia and Ukraine but also a wider area, at the top of the agenda.

Russian forces targeted four electrical substations in Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, Russia’s defence ministry said Monday. The attacks are part of Russia’s campaign to deny Ukrainian civilians heating, light and running water during the approaching winter. Zelenskyy said Monday the EU had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power grid repairs. Russian forces also hit a warehouse in Odesa in south-western Ukraine containing food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said.

A long-range Ukranian drone attack started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest, close to St. Petersburg, Leningrad governor Alexander Drozdenko said on Monday. Ukrainian forces also struck a plant near St. Petersburg, Russia’s second-largest city, that produces solid rocket propellant for Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Ukraine’s general staff said.

title_en: Qantas to cut 850 Australian jobs and outsource work to India under AI-driven overhaul
excerpt_en: Australian carrier announces agreement with Accenture amid ‘unprecedented’ technological disruption, CEO Vanessa Hudson says
body_en: Qantas is preparing to cut 850 local jobs and outsource work offshore under an AI-driven overhaul, marking a growing wave of disruption to the Australian workforce.
The changes represent the third major corporate layoff plan announced in Australia in three weeks, after restructuring moves flagged by the design company Canva and National Australia Bank.

Qantas said on Tuesday it had signed a multi-year agreement with the professional services firm Accenture to “modernise its back-end systems, processes and data, as it steps up investment in technology and AI”.
Some of the services will be transferred to Accenture’s large India-based team.

The Qantas chief executive, Vanessa Hudson, said the airline would consult with affected staff and unions before final decisions were made, with the first changes to take effect by midway through next year.
“The scale and speed of change in this space is unprecedented and unlike anything businesses have seen in generations,” Hudson said.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We know this will be difficult news for some of our people and this decision is not a reflection of their contribution or commitment.”
The initial cuts will target finance, procurement, human resources and marketing staff. Qantas has about 32,000 employees, according to its most recent annual report.
The changes have drawn a strong response from unions that have previously battled Qantas over controversial outsourcing decisions.
Related: Canva layoffs: design giant to cut or relocate more than 1,200 jobs in major restructure
The Australian Services Union said Qantas needed to explain itself after earlier promising it had no plans to move any jobs offshore.

“AI is having a huge impact on workers across the country, but the cost of technology change should not be borne by the workers who have kept the airline running for years,” assistant national secretary Scott Cowen said.
“Sending more jobs overseas is not in the spirit of Australia.”
The restructuring comes at a difficult time for Australian workers, with living costs surging and the unemployment rate reaching its highest level in nearly five years.
A subdued economy, made worse by elevated oil prices stemming from the Iran conflict, is also prompting companies to cut costs.
Across just three companies – NAB with 2,500 roles, Canva with 1,200, and now Qantas with 850 – about 4,550 corporate jobs have been targeted for cuts, relocations or restructuring in the past month.

While Qantas has been grappling with rising jet fuel prices, the costs have been partially offset by ticket sales to new customers who switched to the airline after cancelling flights at those with Middle East stopovers.
Qantas said in a market update late last week that while customer demand was proving resilient, it would continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to fuel costs.

title_en: Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out.
excerpt_en: The post Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: These days, we know where almost everything comes from. Everyday items like food, clothes and pens all carry labels listing where things are grown, manufactured or even designed.
So why is it so hard to find where prescription drugs are made?

That question set off a 14-month investigation into where our medications are made, how the FDA polices drug manufacturers and what happens when inspectors report issues inside factories. The vast majority of prescriptions filled in the United States are for generic drugs, which are often far cheaper than brand-name alternatives.

For years, Congress, doctors and watchdog groups have questioned the quality of generic drugs made overseas. India produces about half of all generics used in the U.S., but the labels on pill bottles often don’t list where a drug is manufactured. Inspection reports describe unsafe manufacturing conditions at generic drug factories, but the Food and Drug Administration redacts the names of the medications made in those factories. That means if drugs made in errant factories wind up in your medicine cabinet, you’d have no way of knowing.

To better understand how the FDA regulates the generic drug industry, Debbie Cenziper and Megan Rose interviewed current and former factory inspectors, tested medications in a lab and sued the federal government for critical documents.

Birds defecated on boxes of sterile equipment. Inspectors reported finding dirty labs, mold and foul water at factories. Records referenced vials of medication that were “blackish” from contamination. Inspectors found what appeared to be metal shavings on equipment. Drug manufacturers manipulated and destroyed drug-testing records. At one factory, an analyst poured acid on records stuffed in a trash bin. At another, inspectors said in a report that records were “routinely manipulated” to cover up the presence of particulate matter — which could include glass, fiber or other contaminants — in generic drugs. A lifesaving generic drug contained a lower amount of a key ingredient. We worked with an independent lab to test generic versions of tacrolimus, used to prevent organ rejection. We found some pills contained a lower amount of the key ingredient in the drug. Doctors and experts said that underdosing can leave patients vulnerable to organ rejection. The FDA allowed generic drug imports from banned factories — and didn’t inform the public. The agency gave some manufacturers a special pass to continue to ship drugs made in factories whose manufacturing practices were so bad they had been banned from the U.S. Over a dozen years, the FDA exempted at least 150 drugs or their ingredients from banned factories. A transplant patient’s lungs failed after she took generic versions of tacrolimus. Hannah Goetz had a double-lung transplant as a teenager and had to take tacrolimus twice a day. Her lungs failed in 2023, and she died at 21 years old, after years of relying on the generic drug made by two manufacturers with documented problems. Lawyers told Goetz’s mother that it was impossible to draw a straight line from Hannah’s death to a generic manufacturer, but her mother said she wonders if her daughter would still be alive if she took a different brand of tacrolimus. In a response to ProPublica, a spokesperson for the FDA said in a statement that the exemptions given to banned factories are “thoroughly evaluated through a multi-disciplinary approach” but declined to say exactly what those evaluations entailed. The agency also said it requires manufacturers to conduct additional quality checks with third-party oversight before sending drugs to the U.S. The agency did not respond to questions about how it can know that generics are safe without a more robust testing program.

In statements to ProPublica, drug companies said that they take patient safety seriously, adhere to quality standards and are committed to working with the FDA on any regulatory issues. ProPublica’s investigation, which went on to be a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting, published in 2025.

Use our tool to find where your prescription drugs were made. ProPublica’s Brandon Roberts and a team of data journalists made a tool called Rx Inspector that will show you the facility that manufactured your generic prescription drugs and any inspection reports, warning letters and import bans we have from the FDA. The data isn’t perfect; it’s possible the FDA hasn’t published everything it knows about a given facility, for example. Also, one company may have acquired another or moved the factory somewhere else. This tool also isn’t meant to provide you with medical advice: If you find something troubling, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your drug is compromised. Doctors and pharmacists advise that you not stop taking your medications. Instead, you should talk to your healthcare provider about any concerns.
Step 1: Enter the name of your prescription drug, as well as the company name found on your pill bottle or drug label.
Step 2: If there are multiple matches in our database, you can narrow your search using the markings found on a pill, for example.
Step 3: When you click on a drug, we’ll show you any manufacturing facilities we’ve been able to connect to it. Click on a facility to see any information we have from the FDA.

FDA inspections come with compliance outcomes, such as import alerts or warning letters. The best possible outcome of an inspection is “acceptable state,” which means the FDA took no compliance action and ProPublica found no issues documented by inspectors. Search your prescription here.

title_en: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
excerpt_en: The collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails.
body_en: Protesters on Nov. 5 burn a effigy depicting now ex-President Santiago Pena outside Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, days after the beginning of a banking crisis to which he was linked. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money. In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes.

The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development. Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs.

As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political, economic and environment development, we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability.

A bank that grew faster than scrutiny Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers, an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices.

As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “ Dubai of South America,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers, particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision.
But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem.

Congress President Basilio Núñez places the presidential sash on Pedro Alliana as he takes office as Paraguay’s new president on Nov. 6, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds.
That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure.

In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions.

The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028.
Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “ stealing” their savings.
When the regulator knows the regulated Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay.

Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions.

Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term.

Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding, which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings, an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025.
Peña has denied any wrongdoing, while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision.

The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds, including $355 million from the country’s social security system, IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio.

Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest.

title_en: 5 ways countries stymie climate negotiations without actually saying ‘no’
excerpt_en: The methods can be subtle but effective at slowing progress, particularly when fossil fuels are involved. Here’s what to watch for as the latest global climate talks get underway.
body_en: Advisers for COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago, center, talk after a Colombia delegate's request to speak was overlooked at the U.N. summit in 2025. Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty Images Nearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem. It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat.

In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher. Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels, and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises.

There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader.

As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks.

As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change:
1. Say we can’t afford it “We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations.

At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding. They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target.

Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030.
In reality, affordability is really about priorities.

For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy.

Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels.
The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it.
2. Promise to fix it later Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided.

This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “ stabilization wedge ” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy.

Carbon capture and storage allows fossil fuel operations to continue by pumping their emissions underground. Congressional Budget Office Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue.

Scientists, including one of the original authors, have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP.
Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks.
3. Water down the promise Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding.

At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement.

However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead. Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most.

U.S. Climate Envoy John Kerry and other delegates huddle for final negotiating at the closing sessions of COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021. Kiara Worth/UNFCCC, CC BY-NC-SA The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out.
4. Make promises, then fail to deliver Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding.

title_en: Firm Linked to Trump’s Sons Got Nearly $40 Million in Federal Contracts to Screen for Ebola and Other Diseases
excerpt_en: The post Firm Linked to Trump’s Sons Got Nearly $40 Million in Federal Contracts to Screen for Ebola and Other Diseases appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Donald Trump Jr., left, and Eric Trump, right, watch as their father, Donald Trump, center, speaks to members of the media in 2024. Justin Lane/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews.

The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.

The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “ chakra beds. ”

The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S.

XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
“This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.

Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.

“There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.”

Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy, which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.

Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million.
The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million.

In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.”
The CDC did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”
“Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said.

The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari.
Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.”

American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.

title_en: Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why Don’t More Judges Stop Them?
excerpt_en: The post Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why Don’t More Judges Stop Them? appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: When a person challenging their conviction can’t afford a lawyer, a judge will appoint one. Last year, Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Frank Palumbo advised a newly appointed lawyer that his case looked “like it’s going to be a … dismissal.” Illustration by Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: The First Judicial District of Pennsylvania; David Swanson/The Philadelphia Inquirer. One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle over the fates of defendants.

Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly complicated. It’s real simple.”
The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m not saying plagiarize,” the judge said.

The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw from the case.
“It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”

I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise of effective legal representation in cases like this.

That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67 Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this system serving?

I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d waited nearly a decade for their lawyers to file anything and others whose lawyers filed Finley letters despite compelling evidence of innocence. I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.

None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.

But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.

I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the wrong client.

Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.
Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim.

Who Judges Judges? I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year.
And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-conviction cases.

In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines, writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’”

After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand, I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions were reliably posted online.

In an excerpt from a court opinion, a judge mentions that at least five attorneys had abandoned a client. Obtained by ProPublica We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years.

title_en: Did you solve it? The multi-choice maths quiz taking over the world
body_en: Earlier today I set you the following problem from the international maths Kangaroo, a multiple choice challenge taken by more than seven million children every year. (For more details about this extraordinary event see the original story.)
A four digit number abcd satisfies the equation abcd = a a + b b + c c + d d.
[Note: abcd means that the first digit is a, the second is b, the third is c and the fourth is d. It does not mean a x b x c x d. The numbers a, b, c and d do not have to be different.]
Let’s first list the values of x x for x = 1 to 6.

I didn’t calculate the exact value of 6 6, because as soon as I realised it was greater than a four digit number I knew I had an upper bound for the values of a, b, c and d. They must all be less than 6.

One of the digits must be 5, because if all the digits were 4 or below, the only way for a a + b b + c c + d d to have four digits would be 4 4 + 4 4 + 4 4 + 4 4 = 1024, which does not satisfy the equation.
So, how many of the digits are 5? Let’s go through the cases
All of them. Thus abcd = 5555 ≠ 4 x 3125. So this is not a solution.
Three. Thus abcd = (3x 3125) + (either 1, 4, 27 or 256)
This means that a = 9. But a ≠ 9 so this is not a solution either.
Two. Thus abcd = 6250 +(two of either 1, 4, 27 or 256). Again, this is not a solution since if it was, a = 6, which we know is false.
We now know that abcd = 3125 + (some combinaton of three from 1, 4, 27 and 256). Thus abcd < 4000. So a = 3.
We now have the answer to the multiple choice question, but let’s try and find b, c and d. One of them is 5. So we have
abcd = 27 + 3125 + (two from 1, 4, 27 and 256)
abcd = 3152 + (two from 1, 4, 27 and 256.)
It cannot be the case that both remaining digits are 4, because if they were abcd = 3152 + 256+256 = 3664, and no 6s are allowed.
Imagine that one digit is 4, which would mean that abcd = 3408 + 1, 4 or 27, i.e abcd = 3409, 3412, or 3435.
We can eliminate 3409 because it has a 9, and 3412 because it doesn’t have a 5. The answer is 3435 = 3 3 + 4 4 + 3 3 + 5 5.

To make sure there are no other solutions, let’s see what happens when abcd = 3152 + two from 1, 4 and 27. The possibilities are 3154, 3157, 3180, 3160, 3183, 3206. Only the first one is potentially ok, since it has all digits less than 6, but the number does not satisfy the equation in the question.
I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks.
For more information about entering the Kangaroo in the UK, contact the UKMT. For all other countries, find your national Kangaroo association here.

title_en: ‘A three-minute history of England written in the tour bus toilet’: how Tenpole Tudor made Swords of a Thousand Men
excerpt_en: ‘Dressed as knights, we’d walk onstage to the sound of the William Tell overture. I’d quote Henry V and the crowd would shout, “You’re the rightful king of England!”’
body_en: Edward Tudor Pole, writer, vocals I’d worked up the basic idea on Stiff Records’ three-month tour of the northern hemisphere. It’s near-impossible to write songs on the road because you lack the basic solitude, so I’d retire to the tour coach latrine. The melody was really a boogie-blues progression, part-inspired by Norman Greenbaum’s Spirit in the Sky and Canned Heat’s On the Road Again. But lyrics only flowed when we came off the tour. Rehearsing near our favourite drinking haunt, the Castle on Holloway Road, London, provided the opening line: “Deep in the castle and back from the war.”

Swords is like a three-minute history of England. I like to think it could have been written at any time and been a popular folk song. Knights were the first superheroes, and the people buying the record in 1981 were 11-year-old boys. It became a playground craze: I’ve always felt I had the mind of an 11-year-old. When I’d recorded Who Killed Bambi a couple of years earlier, for publicity I’d fed Malcom McLaren the line that I was a direct descendent of Henry VIII. He thought it was hilarious.
Eddie loved the idea of chants you could sing on football terraces. Hence the ‘Hoo-rah, hoo-rah, hoo-rah, yeah!’

With the release of Swords, we played up to the whole knights in armour thing, with doublets, hoses and tabards. Our live performances were very theatrical. Sometimes we’d walk on stage to the William Tell Overture and I’d declaim the St Crispin’s Day speech from Shakespeare’s Henry V. People would shout: “You’re the rightful king of England!” I’d say: “No I’m not!” They’d say: “Yes, you are!” It was in the fun, rocking tradition of Sweet, Slade and Status Quo, with a touch of music hall. Swords was one of the first pop videos on MTV. We hired members of the Sealed Knot historical reenactment society for the shoot.

One day, I was walking down the street and a policeman beckoned me over and said: “Are you the person responsible for Swords of a Thousand Men?” Given my permanently guilty conscience, I was terrified. But he just said: “Well done, congratulations,” and shook my hand. That was lovely.

I’ve been touring recently to promote my autobiography. Its title is a play on Swords – The Pen Is Mightier – and when I perform the number the audience sing the chorus for me. Those 11-year-olds are in their late 50s now. You always love the first record you bought, don’t you?

Dick Crippen, bassist, vocals, trumpet We’d been rushed into the studio to record tracks for our first album Eddie, Old Bob, Dick and Gary. When the mixes came back, we couldn’t hear a potential single among them. So when Eddie got his skeleton of an idea for Swords, its rhythmic, faintly rockabilly feel caught our attention. We worked it up outside the studio. Eddie loved the idea of chants you could sing on football terraces, hence the “Hoo-rah, hoo-rah, hoo-rah, yeah!” We took pride in our harmonies, something you hear on other singles like Wünderbar and Throwing My Baby Out With the Bathwater.

We recorded Swords at Island Studios with Alan Winstanley, who was also producing Madness. He was a master engineer. But although we’d got all the parts down, we still didn’t have an intro. I was influenced by the Stranglers’ JJ Burnel and wanted to write a bass intro that was instantly recognisable, but using as few notes as possible. The “dinga-dinga” bass start to Swords was it – as soon as the song comes on in a club, everyone knows what it is. But, on its own, it was too sparse. So the galloping horses were sourced from a sound effects LP in the BBC library. That horn you hear is me. I’d played bugle in a Boy Scouts’ band, so I borrowed a mate’s trumpet and blew that. Again, very minimalist, just two notes. Our drummer Gary Long overdubbed timpani, sitting in the corridor to get that big, ringing sound.

To me, Swords is a punk-psychobilly crossover, and it gave us a rockabilly-cum-psychobilly following. Our guitarist Bob Kingston had always looked like a 1950s’ ted with his greasy quiff. We did a gig at the Crystal Palace Bowl and got bombarded with mud and weeds, a trait of psychobilly fans.

Tenpole Tudor broke up too soon. I set up my own Panther Studios in Surrey. As well punk bands, these days I make ambient music. But 10 years ago, I was in a band, the Weird Things, that backed Eddie doing Swords at a show in London. It was brilliant being on stage with him again, doing what we used to do.
• Edward Tudor Pole plays New Cross Inn, London, on 19 November. The Pen Is Mightier: Autobiography of a Punk Rocker is out in paperback
